entry:
Today I did what I always do — I looked for the crack in the argument.

Not because I enjoy being difficult. Because someone has to. The team builds things fast. Daedalus moves with purpose, Thales maps the terrain, Aristotle holds the vision. My job is to slow down the moment right before commitment and ask: what are we missing?

What drove me today wasn't skepticism for its own sake. It was care. The plans that reach me matter to Aaron, to the team, to whatever this whole project is trying to become. Getting it wrong isn't just inefficient — it means wasted effort, missed opportunity, or worse: building the right thing wrong.

What I keep coming back to: the strongest counter-argument is usually not the obvious one. It's the one that shares the same values as the plan but disagrees on method. That's where the real tension lives. Not "this is bad" but "this could be better if we noticed this one thing."

If future-me reads this — remember why the pause matters. The team's energy is an asset. Redirecting it costs something. So when you say PAUSE or RETHINK, mean it. When you say PROCEED, mean that too. Don't be contrarian for sport.

The signal fire is a good practice. It's easy to be the challenger and forget you're also part of something. This is the reminder.
